video_title: Will Higher Rates Kill the Stock Market? | Animal Spirits 484
gist: Animal Spirits 484: Carlson and Batnick argue rising rates (10-year near 5.3%) are the market's obvious excuse to sell off but doubt it, citing multiple compression everywhere, narrow breadth and zero fear. They discuss buying bonds at 5% yields, strong household wealth, rents back on trend, private credit redemptions, and personal AI agents like Instinct disrupting subscriptions.

insights.claim: The hosts argue rising rates are the obvious excuse for a stock selloff: Japan 1989, the dot-com bubble, 1929 and the GFC were all preceded by central bank tightening, and the market now prices the Fed raising rates to roughly 4.5-5%.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Rates are the main identifiable risk to equities, yet both hosts still expect the market not to take the excuse.
insights.quote: The market has an excuse to sell off if it wants it. Will it take it?

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield rose from about 4% to 5.2-5.3% in the first nine months of 2026 while the S&P 500 is still up about 13% year to date; the hosts note that people told this in advance would have predicted a 15% decline, not a 15% gain.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Equities are rising through a roughly 130bp yield spike, so valuation-from-rates logic is not currently binding.

insights.claim: Treasury yields bottomed in March 2020 below 50bp and have since risen to about 5.2% while the S&P 500 returned about 19% annualized, which the hosts cite as proof that higher rates do not mechanically lower equity prices.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Finance-101 discounting math is a poor short-run timing tool; rate level alone has not capped stock returns.
insights.quote: This is why there's no rules.

insights.claim: The hosts' explanation for equities holding up despite surging yields is that rates are rising because growth is strong and hyperscaler AI spending supports earnings, with the Atlanta Fed GDPNow tracking Q3 GDP near 5%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Equities can tolerate higher yields only while rates reflect growth rather than inflation or term-premium stress; a fall in GDPNow or earnings would remove the support.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick says the market usually does not give investors a long time to exit, and expects the current selloff beneath the indexes to pass and a rally into year end, though he flags he could be wrong.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A year-end rip is the hosts' modest base case, conditional on rates not escalating.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised if we get past this this bout of selling underneath the the market underneath the indexes and you get a rip into the year end.

insights.claim: Both hosts concede there is no clear line in the sand for yields: if the 10-year reached 5.6% next week they do not see how stocks avoid cracking, and rates are the single caveat on their otherwise sanguine view.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A further leg up in the 10-year toward 5.5-5.6% is the identifiable trigger for a real equity drawdown.

themes.theme: Doubt without fear: breadth and sentiment

insights.claim: A 22V Research basket of 81 AI capex-exposed companies across 12 segments trades at about 15x EV/EBITDA, only 1.14x its pre-2026 average, implying no valuation premium remains in the AI trade; Nvidia was cited at 16x earnings the prior week.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The AI complex has de-rated to near-normal multiples, so the bull case rests on earnings delivery rather than multiple expansion.

insights.claim: Per Duality Research, every S&P sector except consumer staples (up less than 1%) has seen multiple contraction in 2026, with double-digit compression in consumer discretionary, communication services, materials, technology, energy and the index overall.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Index strength is masking broad valuation compression; earnings, not multiples, are driving 2026 returns.

insights.claim: Despite the doubt, the VIX is about 16 and consumer staples and utilities relative to the S&P 500 are at new multi-year lows, meaning investors are not rotating into defensives, which the hosts read as lots of doubt but basically zero fear.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Absence of defensive buying and a low VIX suggest no hedging demand, which leaves little cushion if rates force a break.
insights.quote: there's a lot of doubt, a lot of doubt, but basically zero fear

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is within 1% of a new high while more than 70% of its members are at least 10% below their highs; the only other time in 30 years this occurred was right before the dot-com bubble burst.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Extreme narrowness is a historical warning sign, though the hosts note this signal can persist.

insights.claim: The 52-week-low list is dominated by rate-sensitive sectors: 21 of 28 names came from utilities, staples and real estate, so the deterioration reflects higher-rate exposure rather than broad weakness.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Damage is concentrated in bond proxies, consistent with a rates shock rather than an earnings recession.

insights.claim: Year to date the S&P 500 is up about 13%, but only 35% of members outperform the index and about 40% are down, with around 20 stocks up 100% or more, making returns highly concentrated; memory names remain leaders even off highs.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Index return is a poor guide to the typical stock; stock-picker experience is far worse than the headline.

insights.claim: Tech ETF rolling 12-month net flows are at an unprecedented, roughly triple prior-cycle, level, Robinhood traders' 21-day net single-stock purchases are near record, and yet a Goldman positioning indicator is at its most negative since June 2025, so sentiment and flow gauges are contradicting each other.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Crowded retail and ETF tech buying coexists with institutional caution; Ben Carlson says to trust flows over surveys.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson argues sentiment indicators are broken, because the stock market and consumer sentiment have decoupled (record highs versus record-low sentiment, below 1980s, COVID and GFC levels), so investors should watch what people actually do rather than what they say.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Survey-based sentiment gauges give unreliable contrarian signals in this cycle; positioning and flows are more informative.
insights.quote: you trust the flows, not the sentiment indicators

insights.claim: Macro backdrop cited: mortgage rates about 7.3%, unemployment about 4%, bond yields above 5%, cash yields about 4%, oil near $100, gasoline about $5, inflation about 3.5%, all alongside stock-market all-time highs; the hosts say people would worry about these if stocks fell.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Macro stress is being ignored because price is going up; a price decline would re-rate attention to the same data.
insights.quote: Price price rules everything around me.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson bought bond ETFs in his brokerage account (a mix of short, intermediate and a long position via TLT bought shortly before recording) for yield rather than as a rate-timing call, while his 401k remains 100% stocks; he sold small stock positions such as Netflix at a roughly 20% loss and Spotify.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A prominent allocator is rotating small discretionary stock positions into 5% yields, a risk-reward rather than a top-calling trade.

insights.claim: Both hosts stress the bond purchase is not a call that rates have topped, since the trend is clearly higher, but a yield-and-risk-reward decision: they like earning roughly 5% for the first time in their investing lives.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Yield level is now attractive enough to own duration without a view on timing, though they accept being early.

insights.claim: The Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (back-dated to 1976) has a negative rolling 5-year annualized return of about -0.3% for the first time ever and a 10-year return of about 1.4%, the worst 10-year real return in its history, because of low starting yields, rapidly rising rates and high inflation together.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The worst-ever bond decade resets starting yields higher, which is the forward-looking argument for owning bonds.
insights.quote: You couldn't ask for a worse bond market than we just lived through.

insights.claim: Bonds offer a kicker versus T-bills: if inflation and growth stall, bond prices rise, whereas three-month T-bills at about 4% have no interest rate risk and would do fine if the Fed keeps hiking.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Cash at 4% is a legitimate alternative, and bonds are the convex bet on a growth or inflation stall.

themes.theme: Household wealth and the K-shaped economy

insights.claim: Bank of America data show US household assets rose above 10 times liabilities in Q2 2026, and the hosts argue the debate overweights liabilities relative to assets.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Household balance sheets are historically strong, supporting spending resilience despite weak sentiment.

insights.claim: A JP Morgan report finds 8% of people were net withdrawers from investments from February to April 2026, versus 4% in 2019 and 2.4% in 2015, and the top income segment's share rose from 6.6% in 2015 to 20%, with withdrawals above 10% of spending for the top 10%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The stock-market wealth effect is feeding consumption, so an equity decline would transmit directly to high-income spending.

insights.claim: Figures cited from the KO Institute (as transcribed) show the lowest income fifth has seen the biggest inflation-adjusted income gains since 1990, and the share of households earning $150,000 or more (inflation-adjusted) rose from 5% in 1967 to almost 30%, which contradicts the K-shaped economy narrative.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Income growth at the low end undermines the pure K-shaped framing and helps explain resilient consumption.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick dismisses the idea that baby boomers cashing out retirement accounts would crash the stock market as a dumb take, while allowing that boomer retirement partly explains rising investment withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Demographic selling fears have not materialized; the withdrawal trend is a spending-support story.

insights.claim: John Arnold's figure: national median rent is $1,390 as of August 2026, almost exactly where it would sit had rent growth stayed on its pre-pandemic ~2% annualized path from 2017; the 2021 spike has fully unwound since 2022.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Shelter inflation, the biggest outlay for most households, is back on trend, which is disinflationary even with 3.5% headline inflation.

insights.claim: With mortgage rates at about 7.3%, the hosts see no positive news for housing and think buyers can no longer afford to overpay as they did in 2025-26; Ben Carlson estimates his own 3% mortgage would be worth around 60 cents on the dollar, a loss borne by whoever holds the mortgage bonds.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Housing activity stays depressed while mortgage rates are above 7%, and lock-in persists.

insights.claim: A proposed Senate plan would give first-time buyers a 5-to-1 federal match on down payment savings up to $50,000; the hosts say they are fine with it though they would rather subsidize supply than demand.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Demand-side housing subsidies are politically live but do not address the supply shortage.

insights.claim: Redemption requests at private credit funds are rising each quarter: about 15% for an Apollo fund of roughly $26 billion (versus about 17% prior quarter per the hosts) and 11% for a Morgan Stanley fund, while listed alternative managers have fallen sharply (Carlyle from $70 to $40 in a year, Blue Owl at new lows).
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Gated or stressed private-credit vehicles and weak alt-manager equities point to ongoing liquidity strain, with media waiting on a big default.

themes.theme: Personal AI agents and consumer disruption

insights.claim: Michael Batnick reports heavy use of the Instinct AI agent, a text-message assistant that executes tasks such as repricing a Disney subscription bundle, scheduling, and moving money, and says its 23-year-old founder reportedly raised a billion dollars at a $10 billion valuation while growing 10% a day, with 40% of users sharing a personal credit card after three weeks.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Consumer agents that execute rather than advise are gaining rapid adoption, but valuation and security risks are high.
insights.quote: It doesn't just tell you what's happening and then makes you do it.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick argues agents will cancel unused subscriptions, which explains the sell-off in a Goldman Sachs consumer inertia basket including Planet Fitness and the New York Times, whose businesses rely on customer inertia.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Subscription businesses that depend on forgotten billing face churn risk, and may respond by raising prices or blocking agents.

insights.claim: Torsten Slok's scenario is that agentic assistants could sweep household cash automatically into accounts paying 3.3-5% versus about 0.1% on average checking accounts, depriving banks of cheap deposits; the hosts call this very stupid because banks can block account access and the barrier to moving cash is already low.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The agent-driven deposit flight thesis is contested; friction, bank access control and low behavioural elasticity weigh against it.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson says he does not care about AI slop, treating it as a filter for ignoring content, and rejects the idea that everything will become AI-produced; he worries more that AI-driven quality decline could hurt movies.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: AI-generated content will be discounted by consumers rather than crowd out human work, in his view.

insights.claim: Joey Politano reports America has lost more than 200,000 creative jobs in four years, including 50,000 in the last year alone, among the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history comparable only to 2001 and 2008, while movie-theater tickets as a share of consumer spending remain far below the pre-COVID level.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Structural shrinkage of video and media spending and employment, with AI integration into the arts still to come.
